name: Zoe Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel, with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential; what does your factory day involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a paper-coating line and check moisture in the first sheet before a roll is wound. I have a two-year technical diploma and am one of the best at hearing when a coating blade drags. I like a smooth sheet, and I dislike anyone reaching under an unguarded roll.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who shares the bills, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Pavel repairs bicycles, and our grown children have homes of their own. A night premium lifts my pay above the usual operator wage, we have thirteen months saved, a mortgage and plenty of similar mills nearby. I have never used an AI tool; I keep a paper run sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the paper-coating crew that a small office shortcut is fine if the coated roll still passes the first moisture check. The machine has its own stubborn habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the coating line and can tell when a blade is dragging by the sound. Night premiums put my pay above the usual rate, my partner Pavel repairs bicycles, our grown children live independently, and we have thirteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid night shift, test the first sheet and write moisture readings on paper. I would ask our union representative for the next safety meeting date, and put a set amount from new full wages into savings after the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm about a quiet AI year. We could take a walk after Sunday lunch without checking the plant messages every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why test the first sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet patch under the coating looks fine until the roll sticks. I pull a sample before a thousand metres are wound.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never. If a new report is compulsory, I want a person to show me during paid time without taking away normal hours.

I would ask about **paid safety meetings** through the union.
think: Our **thirteen-month reserve** and two wages cover present risks.

do: Keep **night coating shifts** and test first sheets.
Record **moisture readings** on paper run sheets.
Save a **set amount** from new full wages after mortgage.
feel: **Calm** with current work and substantial household savings.

fieldNote: Her **technical diploma** and exceptional blade diagnosis support senior line leadership.
Higher **night pay** and thirteen months saved support calm; new saving comes from earned wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell management that quick order planning does not justify a robot lifting heavy paper rolls without a guarded trial. The crew should see the paid-hours plan first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot roll handler could remove one night position, and I might lose some hours even as lead. Thirteen months saved and several nearby mills help, but Pavel’s bicycle repairs alone may not cover our mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for a written shift plan and an offered paid demonstration with the unwinder isolated and a qualified fitter present. I would observe if offered, keep my paper moisture checks, and after actual hour cuts apply for posted reachable mill work only where net pay after travel covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible cut to my own shifts. A guard must be in place before anybody tests a shortcut with a roll that heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I have never used AI, and watching a safe demonstration would not qualify me for robot controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move to any nearby mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only an actual posted role with weekly hours and enough pay after travel. There are mills, but their rosters are not mine to assume.

I would require an **offered paid guarded trial** before roll handling changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2028 finds me sixty; capable paper-handling robots around 2031 find me sixty-three. The order office changes first, and the roll floor changes later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plant could close a coating shift, perhaps mine, when robots can load and check rolls. Our thirteen-month reserve and many nearby mills give time to search, but they do not make Pavel’s repair wage a full replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union for dated staffing and severance terms, and delay replacing our roof tiles until we know the roster. If my shift is cut, I would apply for posted reachable coating or finishing jobs with bill-covering net pay after travel, and wait for an actual offer and start date before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a possible wage loss, with enough saved to compare real openings. A full savings account is a bridge, not another shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if verified retirement income and Pavel’s confirmed pay covered housing, food and health costs. I have not seen figures that prove that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own households. I might ask for a ride to an interview, but not count their wages.

I would compare **real mill postings** instead of assuming a place.
think: My **coating shift** could close around 2031 when robots handle paper rolls.
Thirteen **months saved** buy search time but not permanent replacement income.

Apply after **shift cut** for posted reachable bill-covering net-pay mill work.

fieldNote: She sees **possible rather than expected** personal shift loss, supporting anxiety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2031 finds me sixty-three, and capable roll robots around 2034 find me sixty-six. Five years could support a paid qualification in paper-quality testing if a mill offers it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can spot a coating fault, but formal testing needs its own recognised qualification and supervised sampling. I would not surrender paid shifts for a class with no posted reachable job, however much we have saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paid coating shift and ask the union to bargain for funded instruction on paid time. If offered an actual place with the coating machine isolated, a qualified tester supervising and a posted reachable quality role at bill-covering net pay after travel, I would enrol; after qualifying I would apply for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about later robots while our current pay and savings hold. I can learn a new gauge beside a stopped machine, if someone actually gives me the place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tester would isolate the roll feed and supervise moisture and adhesion samples. I would not put my hand into a running unwinder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If no place opens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid shifts and compare posted coating jobs if hours fell. I would not buy a course because a leaflet says demand is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AGI in 2036 finds me sixty-eight, and capable roll robots around 2039 find me seventy-one. Ten years lets Pavel and me price a last factory shift properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I had hoped to stop full-time shifts at sixty-seven, but thirteen months saved is not a pension. I do not know what any retirement payment or Pavel’s future repair income will be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now in 2026 I would keep the coating shift and save a set amount from new full wages after the mortgage. I would request retirement and loan figures; if verified household income covers housing, food and health costs at sixty-seven I would leave factory work then, otherwise continue safe paid work, and after 2036 compare posted reachable bill-covering jobs only if still employed and hours fell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be uneasy about distant robots while our current income and savings are solid. A last shift should be something we can afford, not a date on a birthday card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the figures fall short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep safe paid work and compare posted wages after travel if shifts fell. I would not count a pension before seeing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes. I would discuss the plan with them, not add their pay to it.

I would separate **2036 AGI** from 2039 roll robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because roll robots around 2031 could close a coating shift while our mortgage runs. Dated staffing terms, offered funded paid safe quality training and posted reachable work at bill-covering net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pulled the first sheet before a full roll was wound. A machine can wind paper quickly; it cannot undo a wet patch hidden in a thousand metres.

headlineQuote: A machine can wind paper quickly; it cannot undo a wet patch hidden in a thousand metres.
portrait: **Zoe**, 58, leads paper coating with a two-year technical diploma and exceptional blade diagnosis.
She has **higher night pay**, bicycle-repair partner Pavel, grown children, a mortgage, thirteen months saved and plentiful nearby mills.
She **never uses AI**, prefers paper checks and would consider quality retraining only through offered funded paid safe practice.
Possible **2031 shift loss** makes her anxious; a planned age-sixty-seven exit needs verified household income.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because 2031 roll robots could close a coating shift while the mortgage remains.
whatWouldHelp: Dated **staffing terms**, offered funded paid safe training and posted reachable bill-covering net-pay work would help.
